papers.title: Assessing Distributional Covariate Balance After Weighting: A Practical Guide
papers.abstract: Health researchers commonly use weighting methods to improve covariate balance when estimating program and intervention effects from observational data. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) and variance ratios assess particular features of balance but may overlook residual differences elsewhere in the covariate distribution. This paper provides practical guidance for using Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS), Anderson-Darling (AD), and Cramer-von Mises (CVM) statistics as complementary distributional balance diagnostics. In an empirical evaluation of a disease management program, weighting based on a main-effects propensity-score model produced SMD and KS statistics below commonly used or proposed balance thresholds of 0.10 for two continuous covariates, which would conventionally be interpreted as indicating acceptable balance. Nevertheless, permutation tests identified residual distributional differences. Adding quadratic terms for these covariates approximately halved their KS statistics, improved variance balance, and eliminated evidence of residual distributional differences, while leaving the estimated program effect substantively unchanged. Supporting simulations showed that KS, AD, and CVM differed in sensitivity to different forms of distributional discrepancy and that the calibration of resampling-based p-values depended on how the reference distribution was constructed. These findings support a practical approach that combines conventional balance measures, graphical assessment, complementary distributional diagnostics, weighting-model refinement, and outcome adjustment when important residual imbalance remains.

papers.title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.

papers.title: Adaptive Sparsity-Aware Projection-Assisted Spectral Embedding for High-Dimensional Noisy Data with Nonlinear Structures
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose SPASE, an adaptive, sparsity-aware, projection-assisted spectral embedding method for feature extraction from high-dimensional noisy data with underlying nonlinear structures and latent sparsity patterns. We first construct a data-driven projection that adapts to the hidden sparsity patterns and the signal-to-noise ratio, reducing noise-induced distortion of pairwise distances. We then apply kernel-based spectral embedding to the projected data to explore the underlying geometric structure. The key methodological contribution is an energy-based projection selection algorithm that is adaptive to the signal-to-noise ratio and sparsity of the signal representation, while mitigating the impact of noise. On the theoretical side, we show that the resulting embeddings converge to the eigenfunctions of an integral operator associated with the latent signal, and the method can remain effective when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. We demonstrate the empirical performance of the proposed method through simulation studies and real-data applications, showing improved accuracy in downstream tasks such as classification and clustering.

papers.title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
papers.abstract: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

papers.title: Never too LATE: Exploiting restrictions for inference on the Local Average Treatment Effect
papers.abstract: Under the exclusion restriction, independence, and monotonicity assumptions, Imbens and Angrist (1994) show that the Wald estimand is equal to the local average treatment effect (LATE). However, these assumptions entail additional restrictions, which we exploit for inference on the LATE. Specifically, we propose a conditional likelihood ratio test that we show controls asymptotic size uniformly over a large class of data-generating processes. The test has very low computational cost: it requires no simulation and involves solving at most four quadratic programming problems. Monte Carlo simulations show that our test can offer substantial power gains over the Wald and Anderson-Rubin tests, including when the instrument is weak.

papers.title: Sharp High-Dimensional Gaussian Approximations over Rectangles without Covariance Restrictions
papers.abstract: We study how well a sum of $n$ independent random vectors with $p$ coordinates can be approximated by a Gaussian vector with the same mean and covariance. We measure the error over rectangles, so the bounds apply to maxima and simultaneous confidence regions. The coordinates may be arbitrarily dependent, even exactly linearly dependent, and the bounds do not deteriorate as the covariance matrix becomes singular. After standardizing the coordinate variances, bounded or sub-exponential coordinates give the $n^{-1/2}$ sample-size rate up to logarithmic factors, with the size or tail bounds held fixed. The main upper bounds retain the Gaussian expected maximum, improving the rates when the coordinates are strongly dependent. Fourth-moment refinements give further improvements when large observations contribute little to individual coordinate variances. If we instead impose a fixed moment bound of order $q>4$ on the largest absolute coordinate, together with a coordinate fourth-moment bound, the rate becomes $n^{-1/2+1/q}$ up to logarithmic factors. At $q=4$, the slower $n^{-1/4}$ rate is unavoidable, confirming our earlier conjecture. We also allow the bounds on observation size to grow with $n$. Lower-bound examples show that the dependence on sample size, observation size, and Gaussian width is sharp up to logarithmic factors in the regimes studied, and in several regimes the upper and lower bounds match including the logarithmic terms.

papers.title: Randomization protects the average, not the trial: chance covariate imbalance and a calibration of balance $P$ values at the design stage
papers.abstract: Randomization makes the unadjusted treatment-effect estimate unbiased over the allocations a scheme could produce, although it does not balance any single trial. Chance imbalances on strongly prognostic baseline variables directly threaten the validity and regulatory credibility of trial results, yet what design-stage balance $P$ values imply for bias and error rates is seldom stated. We review evidence on chance covariate imbalance and derive that link under a linear model with one normal prognostic covariate, with simulation checks. Given the realized allocation, the unadjusted estimate is biased by $β$ times the difference in covariate means; in standard-error units the bias is $ρZ_{\mathrm{bal}}$, where $ρ$ is the covariate-outcome correlation and $Z_{\mathrm{bal}}$ the balance z-statistic, so it does not shrink as trials grow. Pre-specified ANCOVA removes this bias, change scores reverse it, and non-collapsibility attenuates odds and hazard ratios even under perfect balance. A worst-balance threshold of $P = 1/e$ marks where the Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound reaches 1; under complete randomization the worst of $k$ independent balance $P$ values falls below it with probability $1-(1-1/e)^k$, 0.99 for $k=10$. Any balance $P$ value $\geq 0.317$ keeps the two-sided conditional type I error of the unadjusted test at or below 5% for every $ρ$; at $1/e$ the one-sided error in the favoured direction is at most 4.1%, against 13-33% at $P = 0.05$. Design-stage balance scores should be benchmarked against complete randomization, weighted by external prognostic strength, and reported alongside allocation predictability and a pre-specified covariate-adjusted analysis plan.

papers.title: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches
papers.abstract: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is a popular Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) approach that uses neural networks trained on simulated data--parameter pairs to approximate the posterior given a user-chosen prior. For high-dimensional observations, NPE methods typically approximate the conditional density of the parameter given a user-chosen or learned summary statistic, rather than the entire dataset, due to the curse of dimensionality. However, both approaches face challenges: hand-crafting good summaries for complex models requires considerable effort from scientists, while learning them from massive datasets can be prohibitively computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

papers.title: Variance-adaptive confidence regions for fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with application to LLM evaluation
papers.abstract: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $θ(F_m)=\int h\,dF_m$ of the empirical law $F_m$ of success probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_m$, from independent counts $c_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_i)$, as for a language model run $n$ times per problem. Coverage is at least $1-α$ for every $n$, $m$ and fixed $(p_i)$, simultaneously for all bounded $h$. The variance-adaptive (VA) region tests each candidate mixing law with the conditional variance of the tail counts it implies. This variance is linear in the law, so the region is a linear program, and cell envelopes keep it valid off-grid. Regions calibrated for iid sampling target a super-population law and are conservative for $θ(F_m)$. With all $n$ tail counts, fixed $n$, continuous $h$ and a grid refined as $m\to\infty$, the identification part of VA's width is first-order worst-case optimal, as for any localization with the same index set. Under a rule fixed before the main comparator runs, VA was narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every $n$ (median width ratio 0.60 at $n=128$), but not than the asymptotic, pointwise AMARI interval at $n=128$; on real rollout pools it was wider than both pointwise and Bonferroni-adjusted AMARI at $n\le128$. For $P(p>0)$ and pass@$k$ with $k\gg n$ the data support only lower bounds.

papers.title: Shrink Responsibly: Empirical Bayes in Economics
papers.abstract: Empirical researchers are often interested in the relative causal impact of individuals or institutions such as teachers, schools, hospitals, or neighborhoods. Regression-based estimates of such unit-specific parameters are often noisy; empirical Bayes (eB) methods can help isolate the signal from the estimation noise. This article provides an overview of eB methodology, showing how eB shrinkage can improve compound decisions---such as selecting individuals with the highest causal impacts---even when the working model motivating the shrinkage is misspecified. Not all analyses benefit from eB shrinkage, however, and we discuss which types of causal summaries are best estimated directly and how to do so robustly. We illustrate practical takeaways with a running analysis of public elementary and middle school value-added.

papers.title: Who Is the Regression About? Auditing AI-Labeled Treatments When Effects Differ
papers.abstract: Researchers increasingly regress outcomes on treatments labeled by large language models. When effects differ, OLS averages the effect on the treated (ATT) and on the untreated (ATU), weighting the smaller group more. A label's bias then has two parts: classical attenuation from misclassification, and a selective term when its errors are correlated with the outcome. In LinkedIn postings, the model misses better-paid remote jobs: a precision check passes, yet the remote pay gap is understated by nearly 40 percent, a bias that more data cannot remove. A stratified, blind audit of both labeled groups corrects it and recovers both effects.

papers.title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
papers.abstract: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

papers.title: Schur multipliers, vanishing minors and Gaussian conditional independence
papers.abstract: Conditional independence in a Gaussian vector is the vanishing of almost-principal minors of its covariance matrix $Σ$. A sensitivity analysis replaces $Σ$ by the Schur product $Δ\circΣ$, where the symmetric multiplier $Δ$ differs from one exactly at the changed positions. Such a change generally destroys some conditional independences, and we determine which minors stay zero. A vanishing minor is preserved for every matrix exactly when the corresponding block of $Δ$ has rank one. When variances or covariances change, each almost-principal minor of $Δ\circΣ$ is a polynomial in the amounts added, with minors of $Σ$ as coefficients, and a conditional independence survives every such change exactly when they vanish. In an undirected graphical model, changing variances joins the neighbours of the perturbed vertices, while changing covariances leaves a structure read from the graph by a separation rule, possibly not graphical. Both extend to ancestral graphs, directed acyclic graphs included, and identify the entries that can vary freely. For the other entries, blocks of rank one along a junction tree characterize the multipliers that preserve a decomposable model. A sensitivity analysis can therefore rest on the conditional independence structure after the change, as illustrated on examination marks of 88 students.

papers.title: FARCH: A Functional ARCH Model for Calibrated Prediction Bands
papers.abstract: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with conditional heteroscedasticity, in which the conditional mean and the conditional volatility of the next curve are forecasted jointly and nonparametrically, by reusing a single kernel weighting scheme --- built on a wavelet semi-metric between curves --- first on the curves themselves and then on their squared residuals. From this pair of estimators we derive two constructions of prediction bands: a pointwise band, obtained from marginal scenario quantiles, and a uniform, sup-norm band, calibrated for decisions that concern the entire forecasted path rather than any single instant. Applied to day-ahead forecasting of half-hourly French national electricity demand (1996--2009), and compared, under an identical protocol, against four existing prediction-interval constructions that do not model the conditional variance explicitly, the uniform FARCH band attains pointwise coverage statistically indistinguishable from its nominal target at the 80%, 90% and 95% levels, and a curve-wise coverage of 90.1%, significantly above the 70.8% reached by the best competing method, at the cost of a wider interval. Pointwise bands, in contrast, undercover regardless of whether the variance is modelled explicitly, indicating that state-dependent volatility and simultaneous calibration are two distinct ingredients that a trustworthy prediction band must combine.

papers.title: A General Theory of Nonparametric Response-Adaptive Randomization
papers.abstract: Response-Adaptive Randomization (RAR) assigns incoming patients to treatments with probabilities that depend on previously observed responses. While most existing RAR procedures rely on finite-dimensional summaries of treatment performance (such as rates, means, or model parameters), we develop a nonparametric (NP) distribution-based framework in which the treatment outcome distributions are learned sequentially and adaptation is driven by their functionals. The framework naturally accommodates multiple treatments and is particularly suited to endpoints for which average effects may conceal relevant differences across the outcome distribution. We introduce an ethical NP-RAR rule driven by a pre-specified distributional score and a nonparametric extension of the multi-arm efficient randomized adaptive design (NP-ERADE) able to approach generic distribution-dependent targets selected according to ethical or inferential optimality criteria. We establish strong consistency and joint functional central limit theorems for the empirical treatment distributions, together with asymptotic normality of functional scores, estimated targets and allocation proportions. We further show that the NP-ERADE allocation proportions attain the semiparametric efficiency bound for the target. We develop post-trial inference for score contrasts and distributional features, including crossing locations, and investigate finite-sample properties, robustness and inferential performance via simulations.

papers.title: Anytime Valid Conformal Prediction on Streaming Time Series
papers.abstract: Sequential prediction on streaming time series is essential for continuous monitoring and risk control in applications such as finance, energy, and healthcare systems, where prediction intervals must remain valid at arbitrary stopping times and adapt to potential distributional shifts. Conventional conformal prediction provides model-agnostic uncertainty quantification but relies on exchangeability, which is violated under distributional shifts. Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI) relaxes this assumption by updating the miscoverage level in response to the realized prediction errors, but it only guarantees that the realized average miscoverage rate along a single trajectory approaches the target level in the long run. Risk-sensitive monitoring instead requires controlling the true miscoverage rate, i.e., the conditional probability that a prediction set misses, which measures the reliability of the set itself rather than the misses that happened to be realized. We show that, without assumptions on the distributional shifts, it is impossible to have such control for every single prediction set at arbitrary stopping times. We therefore target the true running and rolling average miscoverage rates. Our methods combine ACI with anytime valid confidence sequences. With high probability, the true running average miscoverage rate stays below the target level uniformly over time, and so does the true rolling average for any window rule. The efficiency loss for the rolling average vanishes for windows that grow sufficiently fast, but not for fixed windows.

papers.title: Renewable Estimation for Generalized Nonparametric Regression with Dynamic Spline Bases and Likelihood Pullback
papers.abstract: Streaming datasets require statistical models to be updated as new observations arrive, often without repeated access to the full history. In generalized nonparametric regression, a fixed spline space may limit approximation accuracy when the initial representation is insufficient. However, when the basis is expanded, the historical summaries represented in the previous spline space must be re-expressed in the enlarged spline space, which requires a suitable mechanism. We propose a renewable penalized-likelihood algorithm for canonical exponential-family nonparametric regression that combines nested cubic-spline refinement with a Gram-metric pullback of the retained historical likelihood quadratic under the streaming setting. The algorithm incorporates incoming-batch likelihood contributions and updates historical score and curvature summaries at the actual fitted center. The Gram-metric pullback preserves the retained historical quadratic over the embedded previous space. Under explicit regularity and algorithmic conditions, we establish L2-consistency at rate O_p(N^{-2/5}) for a fixed target in H^2[0,1]. We further establish that the energy-norm discrepancy between the renewable estimator and a matched offline estimator is of smaller order, where the offline method is fitted based on the full data and using the same realized terminal spline space and penalty. Simulations demonstrate the benefits of dynamic bases when the initial spline representation is restrictive, with additional gains from historical summary pullback. Additional experiments assess computational cost and storage of the proposed method relative to the offline method. Applications to real datasets also illustrate the proposed method.

papers.title: Optimal Importance Sampling Densities for Estimating Several Expectations at Once
papers.abstract: Simulation studies often estimate several quantities from a single sample, and the best importance sampling density depends on how the errors on these quantities are combined. We characterise the optimal auxiliary density for a general error criterion. We show that it is the nominal density reweighted by a weighted length of the vector of estimated functions, where the weights are set by the error criterion, or by the curvature of the loss when the criterion comes from a loss on the errors. We also provide a lower bound on the best achievable error. The optimal density is explicit for smooth losses, including the usual losses on covariance matrices. We also derive allocation laws for the cells of a histogram and characterise the minimax density for the probabilities of several events. When there is no closed form, we show how to compute the optimal density numerically.

papers.title: A conic optimization framework for shape-constrained functional regression analysis
papers.abstract: Standard regression methods do not always guarantee that the estimated model reflects prior knowledge about how predictors relate to the response, which motivates constrained regression. When the effects to be estimated are smooth nonlinear functions, a natural family of constraints is that of shape constraints, such as sign, monotonicity, or curvature, which encode qualitative properties that these functions are often expected to satisfy. While shape-constrained estimation of smooth functions is well established in classical regression with scalar covariates and response, its extension to functional regression, where the coefficients are themselves functions, remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose the functional shape-constrained conic P-spline estimator (FunSCOPE), a unified framework for shape-constrained functional linear regression that covers scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and function-on-function models, and in which any combination of the shapes above can be imposed on the functional regression coefficient. Building on a P-spline approach, the desired shapes are expressed as conditions on the scalar regression coefficients, which leads to an estimation problem formulated as a conic optimization problem. For univariate coefficients, as in scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and a particular case of the function-on-function regression, the concurrent case, these conditions are both necessary and sufficient, in contrast to existing approaches, which provide only sufficient conditions; for bivariate coefficients, as in general function-on-function models, they are neither necessary nor sufficient. Numerical experiments show that FunSCOPE outperforms competing methods in terms of estimation error and computational time.

papers.title: Do Hierarchical Networks Actually Learn? Insights from Word-of-Mouth Estimation
papers.abstract: We study recursive estimation of a constant state vector by a hierarchical network of asymmetrically informed linear estimators, modeled as a directed tree. Only the leaves observe the regression signal, whereas every other estimator learns by word of mouth from noisy signal estimates relayed by its children. Authority within the hierarchy is expressed through common prior information: after each round, every estimator adopts the estimate and error covariance broadcast by the root. The more accurate this common information, the larger the effective noise variance on local observations, which makes estimation intrinsically self-defeating. The resulting performance is the subject of this paper. We show that recursive least-squares (RLS) estimators do learn the state in mean square, albeit slowly. Under strong persistency of excitation, the broadcast error covariance decays polynomially in time, at a rate that we characterize by upper and lower bounds of matching order. The exponent is determined by the smallest number of relays between a leaf and the root, and it decreases exponentially with this number.

papers.title: Bayesian variable selection via collapsed importance-weighted variational inference over discrete model spaces
papers.abstract: Bayesian variable selection under spike-and-slab priors provides interpretable posterior inclusion probabilities for individual predictors, but exploring large discrete model spaces using conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo methods can be computationally challenging. We develop a collapsed importance-weighted variational framework for Gaussian linear regression. The framework analytically integrates out the remaining model parameters and directly approximates the posterior over binary inclusion indicators using a factorised Bernoulli distribution. To improve posterior inclusion probability estimation while retaining the computational simplicity of the factorised variational family, we replace the conventional evidence lower bound with a tighter variational Rényi importance-weighted lower bound. We establish a finite-sample upper bound on posterior inclusion probability approximation errors and show that, under suitable conditions, the optimised variational inclusion probabilities converge to their exact posterior counterparts as the number of importance samples increases and the Rényi parameter decreases appropriately. We further establish that analytical marginalisation tightens the variational objective and the corresponding inclusion probability error bound, while reducing importance-weight variance and improving the asymptotic efficiency of importance-sampling post-processing. To address the challenges of estimating gradients with respect to the variational parameters when the inclusion indicators are discrete, we leverage recent advances in variance-reduced score-function estimators, together with an annealing strategy to stabilise optimisation. Simulation experiments and empirical applications demonstrate improvements in posterior inclusion probability estimation relative to standard variational inference and two existing variational approaches.

papers.title: Semiparametric regression with stagewise empirical risk minimization
papers.abstract: Maintaining both interpretability and accuracy remains a fundamental challenge in regression analysis. This paper addresses these two objectives through a semiparametric approach that combines a parametric crude guess with its nonparametric adjustment. In particular, the nonparametric adjustment is implemented via a machine learning technique called ``stagewise empirical risk minimization algorithm.'' Once a set (dictionary) of functions (words) is prepared, this algorithm constructs a convex combination of words selected iteratively from the dictionary. This selection is based on the empirical risk derived from the Bregman divergence, which enables the proposed estimators to be applied in broad settings, including generalized linear models. This paper examines these proposed semiparametric estimators theoretically and numerically. In the theoretical study, we derive a non-asymptotic error bound for the estimators constructed from a general data-dependent dictionary. Among the concrete dictionaries proposed in this paper, some can be utilized to correct variable selection in LASSO-based parametric regression, which is investigated in the numerical study. Moreover, simulation studies investigate practical performance of the proposed estimators, while real data applications further confirm their predictive performance. These studies indicate that the proposed semiparametric estimators can address the above challenge in several settings.

papers.title: Two-Stage Staffing with Random Arrival Rate: A Simulation Optimization Approach
papers.abstract: In service systems, the arrival rate in the same time period and day of the week exhibits randomness, yet can be more accurately estimated or forecast right before that period, which motivates a two-stage staffing scheme with advance base staffing and pre-shift surge staffing. Existing approaches usually impose strong assumptions on the arrival process and service systems' operational logic and other further approximations (i.e., stylized models) to derive explicit staffing policies. This paper proposes a simulation optimization approach (SOA) for more general arrival processes and service systems by effectively addressing some intertwined challenges. By recasting the original formulation into computationally tractable structures and designing an efficient coordinate-search algorithm, it constructs a two-stage staffing lookup table offline, which allows managers to make real-time surge staffing decisions without any further simulation. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed SOA has significantly better staffing performance and substantially broader applicability compared to existing approaches. Even under the stylized models, the cost savings delivered by our SOA compared with existing approaches range from the low tens to several tens of percent, depending on different problem parameters; the advantage further amplifies when the actual problem deviates from the stylized models. In a nurse-staffing case study grounded in real-world data, the proposed SOA delivers approximately 8% to 13% cost savings over a state-of-the-art benchmark.

papers.title: multiCAsp: Spatially Informed Canonical Association Analysis of Multi-Omic Data
papers.abstract: Simultaneous profiling of multiple molecular layers at spatially resolved locations creates opportunities to identify shared cross-modal biological variation in its tissue context. We present multiCAsp (multi-omic Canonical Association informed by spatial graph), a probabilistic latent-factor model for integrating $M \geq 2$ spatially resolved omic modalities. It incorporates spatial dependence through a graph-Laplacian prior on shared latent factors and uses an expectation-maximization algorithm to estimate factor scores and modality-specific feature loadings. Because the prior is defined on a neighborhood graph rather than on Euclidean distances, it accommodates irregular tissue geometries and extends naturally to multiple tissue sections. Simulations show that multiCAsp consistently achieves higher mean latent subspace and loading recovery than alternative methods across varying sample sizes, feature dimensions, and noise levels, with the largest gains under high noise. Compared with an existing Gaussian process-based spatial factor model, it is also less sensitive to how the spatial coordinates are represented, produces spatially smoother factors, and has lower computational cost. Applied to metabolomic-proteomic data from macaque cortex and gene-protein data from human renal carcinoma, multiCAsp recovers spatially coherent multi-omic factors with interpretable biological signatures. In the macaque data, transferred factors retain broad spatial patterns across animals and support cross-modal prediction of protein abundances from metabolomic measurements.

papers.title: Nonsense rank correlations between independent random walks
papers.abstract: Yule's nonsense correlation persists for Spearman's rho and Kendall's tau between independent random walks. Neither coefficient concentrates at zero as the sample size grows. For centred random walks with finite increment variances, we derive a universal joint limit expressed through Brownian occupation functionals. Integral formulas give limiting variances of approximately 0.222 and 0.108, respectively, below the Pearson value of 0.241. Rank correlations thus reduce the limiting dispersion on their respective coefficient scales. We prove that both marginal limits have symmetric densities and represent them exactly as limits of polynomial densities determined by Gaussian moment integrals. Spearman's conventional t test and Kendall's normal approximation are asymptotically invalid, with rejection probabilities tending to one under process independence.

papers.title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.

papers.title: False Discovery Rate Control in Ordered Sequential Testing: Rejection-Count and Fallback Procedures
papers.abstract: We study false discovery rate (FDR) control for a fixed family of hypotheses tested sequentially in a prespecified order. Each decision uses only the current and preceding $p$-values, is not subsequently revised, and permits continued testing after non-rejections. We distinguish generalized fixed-sequence procedures based on preceding rejection counts from fallback-type procedures that additionally use recursively transferred testing levels. For rejection-count procedures, we study a position-dependent calibration under independence and a linear rule calibrated through null marginal distribution functions under positive left-tail dependence under the null. We clarify their connections to existing fixed-sequence and online FDR methods. The fallback construction combines the total number of preceding discoveries with level transfer along consecutive rejections, allowing thresholds to reflect the arrangement of earlier outcomes. We establish its FDR control under history-based positive regression dependence and, with a position-specific correction, under arbitrary dependence. For all four constructions, the guarantees extend to every deterministic testing time within the planned horizon. Gaussian simulations assess the effects of signal placement, dependence, and allocation weights. They demonstrate power gains over selected benchmarks while identifying the conservativeness of the arbitrary-dependence correction.

papers.title: Decorrelation Before Variable Selection: Left and Right Transforms and Their Trade-Off
papers.abstract: Decorrelation has two forms. A left transform keeps coefficients and changes noise; a right transform keeps noise and changes coefficients. Cholesky whitening alone keeps noise variables inactive when true ones come first; decorrelation preserving coefficients and noise loses information.

papers.title: Maximum Scores and Treatment Feedback in Regression Discontinuity Designs
papers.abstract: Hospitals use repeated risk scores to decide when to send an alert. Some evaluations summarize these scores by their maximum and use the maximum as the running variable in a regression discontinuity (RD) design. The maximum shows correctly whether a patient was ever alerted. However, it can include scores recorded after an earlier alert has already changed care. In this paper, we study what the maximum-score RD estimates when an earlier intervention changes a later score. We use a two-assessment model and derive a formula that splits the RD contrast into the causal effect and a composition term. When feedback moves scores in one direction, the composition term equals the relative jump in the density of the maximum at the cutoff times a prognostic contrast. Therefore, an exactly continuous density means no bias, and the population density jump bounds the bias. Valid inference on the jump turns this into a confidence bound under a stated sensitivity assumption. Within this model, bias behind a continuous density requires feedback in both directions. For this case, we bound bias by total boundary movement and construct conservative confidence sets for binary outcomes under explicit sensitivity and smoothness assumptions. We give closed forms for independent uniform scores and for correlated Gaussian scores. In one example, a true risk reduction of four percentage points appears as a one-point increase. Simulations confirm the formulas. Narrower bandwidths, robust bias correction, and machine-learning covariate adjustment do not remove the bias. A fuzzy RD on the first score recovers the causal effect when early and late treatment have the same effect. Our results concern how the running variable is built. We do not assess any published clinical study.

papers.title: Medicaid Quality Disparities: Domain-Specific Performance Analysis and Approaches for State-Level Improvement
papers.abstract: Medicaid covers nearly 78 million people, yet care quality varies across states, programs, and clinical domains. Using the 2024 CMS Child and Adult Core Sets (9,781 usable state-measure observations from 11,100 records), this study combined descriptive statistics, benchmark-gap analysis, correlation, and OLS regression to find where shortfalls cluster. Disparities were strongly domain-specific. Maternal and Perinatal Health scored lowest (28.0%), followed by Dental and Oral Health (38.5%) and Behavioral Health (44.4%), while Long-Term Services and Supports (82.8%) and Experience of Care (67.8%) scored highest. State performance correlated strongly with national benchmarks (r = 0.77, approximately), so rates should be read against each measure's benchmark. Domain was the strongest predictor, and the model explained 31.2% of variance. Because of heteroscedasticity and influential observations from mixing bounded and utilization measures, estimates are descriptive. Quality improvement should be targeted by domain, prioritizing maternal health, behavioral health network adequacy, and dental provider participation.

papers.title: Beyond AUC: Do Mammography Risk Models Predict When Cancer Occurs?
papers.abstract: Longitudinal deep learning models for mammography-based breast cancer risk prediction output either per-year cumulative risks or a discrete distribution over the year of diagnosis, from which cumulative risks F1,...,F5 are derived. These models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and the concordance index. We show that these metrics are largely insensitive to when cancer occurs: they can be high even for a model that carries no information about the year of diagnosis. We re-evaluate two recent longitudinal models (OA-BreaCR, LMV-Net) on CSAW-CC with a 5-year horizon using timing metrics computed on cancer cases only. Despite C-indices up to 0.75, neither orders cancer cases by time to diagnosis significantly better than chance (c_time 0.51 and 0.55, both 95% CIs covering 0.5). Weighted absolute timing error favours a constant "year 3" prediction over both models, so we use c_time as the primary timing metric. For Mirai's additive-hazard head, also used by LMV-Net, we analyse how per-year increments passed through a ReLU can collapse under severe class imbalance. We also propose a breast-level, two-stage model that separates whether from when. It matches LMV-Net in discrimination (C-index 0.745 vs. 0.746) but orders cancer cases better (c_time 0.58 vs. 0.51, paired 95% CI of the difference 0.01-0.13), on par with Mirai's published weights (0.57).

papers.title: Scaling large language model-assisted line-of-therapy adjudication with human-in-the-loop evidence-calibrated selection
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the ability to scale clinical adjudication tasks traditionally dependent on exhaustive manual review. Line-of-therapy (LoT) adjudication, a major bottleneck in oncology cohort construction, is a prime example. Line boundaries must be inferred from longitudinal treatment histories according to nuanced, study-specific definitions, at every regimen transition for every patient. LLMs can apply this adjudication at scale, but their reliability varies across patients. Treatment histories differ in complexity, and ambiguous or atypical patterns depend on expert clinical judgment. Reliable automation thus requires verified support for model assignments and the ability to identify cases that warrant manual review. Here, we present evidence-calibrated selection (ECS), a human-in-the-loop framework for scaling LLM-assisted LoT adjudication. ECS derives confidence from observed clinician adjudications, prioritizes patients with the least-supported assignments for follow-up review, and returns completed adjudications to the model as precedent. As the evidence base grows, ECS continuously calibrates confidence to estimate residual error, thus enabling more efficient use of clinician time. In simulations on 136 clinician adjudicated patients with multiple myeloma, ECS achieved a residual error of 5% after review of 44.6% of patients, compared to 62.2% when review was directed by LLM self-reported confidence and 81.9% under random sampling. These results support a scalable approach to study-specific LoT adjudication, using clinician evidence to inform automated predictions, minimize error, and reduce review burden.

papers.title: Improving Tropical Cyclone Forecasts through Objective Ensemble Track-Error Reduction
papers.abstract: Accurate tropical cyclone (TC) track guidance is essential for warnings, evacuation planning, and risk communication, but outlying members and distinct track scenarios can degrade raw ensemble forecasts. Statistical and machine-learning (ML) methods proposed to improve ensemble guidance are difficult to compare because previous studies often use different forecast systems, basins, periods, and verification methods. Using a common verification framework, this study compares six objective methods (four statistical trimming and two ML methods) with the full ensemble mean for 138 TCs forecast by GEFS, MOGREPS-G, and IFS during 2016-2024. Dynamic trimming (DT) is the most consistent statistical method, reducing mean total track error by 8.0%, 13.4%, and 16.1% at short, medium, and long ranges. Its largest benefits occur in high-spread cases, where it can reach 70% of the low-error bound. Short-lead-error trimming (SLET) provides useful delayed guidance after early observations become available, but its improvement decreases with lead time. Regression-mixture clustering (RC) shows potential in low-spread cases and provides the largest improvement over the control run. The gradient boosted tree (GBT) produces the largest medium-range improvement and exceeds the theoretical trimming bound, suggesting strong potential, particularly when the observed track is poorly represented by the ensemble family. However, its 12.8% short-range degradation and gains concentrated in a small subset of cases indicate overcorrection when the ensemble mean is already accurate, highlighting the need for additional constraints. These results provide a consistent basis for using objective error-reduction methods to strengthen TC track guidance for operational decision-making.

papers.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis for Ordinal Functional Data with Application in Diabetes Intervention
papers.abstract: Traditional functional principal component analysis (FPCA) is typically designed for continuous functional observations. In this paper, we address the scenario where the outcome consists of repeated categorical data defined over a bounded interval. Our objective is to develop an FPCA methodology tailored specifically for ordinal functional data. Our approach leverages recent advancements in ordinal data modeling to estimate both the mean function and the eigenfunctions, while employing a computationally efficient method for predicting the scores. The performance of the proposed methodology is evaluated numerically in simulation and data application on diabetes intervention.

papers.title: Knowing Less After a Diagnostic Test: Dilation in Clinical Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Dilation (Seidenfeld and Wasserman 1993) occurs when conditioning on new information \textit{only} increases uncertainty regardless of what the information reveals. Often viewed as an undesirable feature of models of ambiguity, dilation has sparked sustained debate about belief updating. This paper shows that following established clinical guidance can induce dilation, even for diagnostic tests that meet conventional performance benchmarks. We characterize when a test is dilation-inducing and show that a ubiquitous feature of performance studies -- evaluating tests against an imperfect reference -- creates scope for dilation. To facilitate detection before clinical use and inform regulatory standards, we develop a finite-sample valid hypothesis test of the null that a diagnostic test is dilation-inducing in this context. Applying the method to an influential study that preceded and contributed to the clinical adoption of chest CT screening for COVID-19, we find that the data are consistent with dilation.

papers.title: Automated Left Ventricle Strain Analysis from DENSE MRI
papers.abstract: Background: Quantifying myocardial strains from Displacement ENcoding with Stimulated Echoes (DENSE) MRI provides insight into left ventricular performance, but current data processing pipelines remain limited in automation, robustness, and full left ventricle coverage. Methods: We present a fully automated framework for voxel-wise displacement and strain analysis of the left ventricle from DENSE MRI. Our method integrates a multi-channel nnU-Net model trained on both magnitude and phase images for segmentation, an automated phase unwrapping approach, an adaptation of the regularized spatiotemporal least squares (RSTLS) formulation for displacement computation, and strain calculations based on radial basis function interpolation. The proposed framework enables the estimation of displacements and strains across the left ventricle from a full stack of short-axis images. Results: Validation using a computational phantom shows the framework's overall resilience to data noise. Following computational phantom evaluation, the proposed framework is applied to analyze DENSE MRI short-axis slices acquired in forty-seven (N=47) healthy volunteers and covering the full left ventricle. Circumferential, longitudinal, and radial strains are presented throughout the cardiac cycle and at peak systole, showcasing the performance of the proposed framework. Results show that circumferential and longitudinal strains are computed accurately. However, challenges persist when estimating radial strain, especially in the subendocardial layer. A group-wise strain comparison is also performed based on volunteers' sex and age showing a significant effect of sex on circumferential and longitudinal strains. Conclusions: Overall, the proposed framework provides an automated and modular pipeline to compute displacements and strains from DENSE MR images that can be scaled and generalized toward clinical applications.

papers.title: Radar Waveform Design via Convex Semidefinite Relaxation
papers.abstract: The ambiguity function (AF) of a radar waveform describes its ability to resolve targets in range and Doppler. Designing a waveform that attains a prescribed AF magnitude is a phase retrieval problem with four trivial ambiguities, and a time- or band-limited pulse is determined up to these ambiguities by at most three times as many AF samples as it has time samples or frequencies. Existing solvers for the narrowband AF, however, are non-convex: they cannot guarantee that they reach the global minimizer, which is unique only up to the trivial ambiguities, so the recovered pulse depends on the starting point. This letter addresses this gap by lifting the problem to positive semidefinite matrices supported on the pulse band, where each AF sample becomes the magnitude of a linear functional. In the lifted space, recovery is formulated as a convex program, and a dual certificate provides a sufficient condition for exactness. The proposed algorithm, wavex, combines an initialization by relaxed reflections, convex semidefinite surrogate steps, and a local polish. Numerical experiments show that wavex accurately recovers band-limited pulses from complete AFs and from AFs with most of their samples removed, provided the remaining samples determine the pulse, and that its accuracy degrades gracefully as the noise increases. wavex is built on the open-source library invexapi, and the code that reproduces every result is available at https://github.com/samuelpinilla/waveX.

papers.title: From the possible to the optimal: differentiable optimization of gene regulatory networks
papers.abstract: Understanding the space of ``the actual and the possible'' regulatory architectures capable of realizing biological functions is one of the major challenges in biology. Optimization-based approaches can rationalize regulatory mechanisms from functional objectives and constraints, but their computational cost has limited them to finding individual solutions. Here, we introduce \texttt{jaxgrn}, a framework that combines differentiable programming with stochastic simulations of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) to optimize thousands of networks end-to-end on GPUs. Using morphogen-driven embryonic patterning as a case study, we optimize networks for domain formation and positional information, while varying constraints on input noise, boundary precision and scaling with system size. While recovering known archetypes for scaling, we find that varying the constraints organizes optimal solutions into qualitatively distinct regimes. When optimizing domain formation, we observe phenotypic convergence across a continuum of regulatory architectures, ranging from input-driven to feedback-driven networks. When optimizing positional information, solutions are initially phenotypically diverse despite moderate variation in regulatory architecture; imposing scaling drives both phenotypic and regulatory convergence of the optimized networks onto a few recurring regulatory architectures. Our systematic approach opens the door for variational systems biology in which changing functional constraints reshape the landscape of possible phenotypes and regulatory architectures.

papers.title: Assessing Subgroup Heterogeneity in Carryover Effects: A Simulation Study and an Observational Alzheimer Disease Treatment-Transition Application
papers.abstract: Subgroup heterogeneity in carryover effects is not routinely evaluated in 2x2 crossover studies, and its inferential consequences remain insufficiently characterized. When the scientific question concerns subgroup-specific carryover, omission of the corresponding interaction causes the fitted model to target a collapsed population-average contrast rather than the subgroup difference of interest. We used simulation to evaluate the finite-sample bias, confidence-interval coverage, Type I error, and power of carryover-by-subgroup interaction inference under an independence-based analysis and REML-based MMRM analyses with CS and UN covariance specifications. Reduced mean models were included as population-average benchmarks. We also applied the models to observational Alzheimer disease treatment-transition sequences from NACC, where carryover was defined operationally as a model-based association with the preceding regimen rather than an identified pharmacologic persistence effect. Full models directly estimated subgroup-specific carryover heterogeneity, whereas reduced models estimated a collapsed carryover contrast that did not characterize this heterogeneity. Under the full mean model, point-estimate bias was small, whereas covariance misspecification affected empirical confidence-interval coverage and Type I error. Reliable inference on subgroup-specific carryover effects requires a mean model that explicitly represents the heterogeneity of interest and a covariance structure appropriate for the repeated-measures data. Failure to address either component can obscure subgroup differences or compromise statistical inference. These results provide practical guidance for evaluating heterogeneous carryover effects in crossover and treatment-transition studies.

papers.title: A plug-in energy-balance freezing module for transformer frost nowcasting without leaf-sensor inputs
papers.abstract: Frost protection requires local warnings where leaf-sensor inputs are unavailable. In the frost literature we surveyed, physics entered machine-learning models through inputs, numerical-model coupling, or losses, rather than model structure. We develop a transformer-compatible module that embeds leaf energy-balance physics in freezing-probability forecasts: an energy-balance temperature reference and a learned residual predict leaf temperature, which drives a multiplicative gate imposing a temperature-dependent probability cap. We mathematically prove conditional monotonicity and an alarm boundary, and test whether placing the same information in the output pathway or in attention yields different benefits. We evaluated 12 hourly leads at 19 Korean stations over five frost seasons, with and without leaf-sensor inputs. In the 2025-2026 hold-out season without these inputs, our time-token transformer (PET-E) achieved a lead-mean critical success index (CSI) of 0.516 versus 0.478 for fixed-configuration, joint-lead LightGBM, with significant gains at all 12 leads, and the fraction of alarms at observed leaf temperatures of at least 2 degrees C fell from 0.087 to 0.051 relative to the unmodified backbone. Across the hold-out and a retrospective 2024-2025 evaluation, the module reduced Brier scores and warm-surface alarm fractions in both the time-token transformer and iTransformer, with no significant CSI decrease at any lead. At held-out stations without static or leaf-sensor inputs, both module-equipped backbones exceeded LightGBM at all 12 leads (CSI 0.468 and 0.467 versus 0.437). In the time-token backbone, the temperature pathway reduced this alarm fraction in all four settings, whereas the attention prior increased CSI in three. These findings link an explicit temperature-dependent probability cap to improved forecasts and distinguish output-side from attention-based embedding.

papers.title: Honest confidence sets under experiment-level failure
papers.abstract: An experiment-level failure replaces the joint observation law while preserving the target. We study honest confidence sets when a declared upper bound on failure probability equals the allowed noncoverage probability. For a Uniform support endpoint and a Gaussian mean on fixed compact parameter intervals, every honest deterministic procedure has full-range worst-case expected diameter under arbitrary or absolutely continuous joint failures. Independent randomisation gives sharp minimax risks of $(2+o(1))\log N/N$ for the endpoint in $[1,2]$ and $(2σ+o(1))(\log N/N)^{1/2}$ for the mean with known variance $σ^2$. A failure distribution shared by many targets forces average clean-state noncoverage to decrease with expected diameter. One-sided local Kullback--Leibler bounds then yield lower bounds with logarithmic factors. The endpoint experiment also has a sharp deterministic frontier as the remaining error budget vanishes. Under exchangeable failures without ties, observation order recovers both randomised benchmark rates deterministically. In a reference-calibrated roster, we derive the randomised minimax reliability rate. A prespecified reference reserve of logarithmic size permits deterministic attainment of the same order on a subclass whose conditionally independent reserved responses have probabilities bounded away from zero and one in every state.

papers.title: Weighted conformal prediction under covariate shift: process limits, estimated weights and efficiency
papers.abstract: Weighted split conformal prediction handles covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio $v=dQ_X/dP_X$; its training-conditional coverage is a functional of the self-normalized weighted empirical distribution function $\hat F_m$, and we study the process $\sqrt m(\hat F_m-F_Q)$. It converges in $\ell^\infty$ to the Gaussian process $W(G(t))-F_Q(t)W(K^2)$, with $G(t)=\mathbb{E}_Q[v\mathbf{1}\{S\le t\}]$ and $K^2=1+χ^2(Q\|P)$, if and only if $χ^2(Q\|P)<\infty$ (for non-degenerate scores); $\sup v$ plays no role. The limit gives the joint law of the coverage across levels, consistent bootstraps, inflations asymptotically exact uniformly in the level, and Berry-Esseen-type rates. With estimated ratios, a uniform expansion remains valid when the estimate uses the calibration covariates; the estimation error enters through a covariance term that can reduce the variance below the oracle's, and a pairs bootstrap reproduces it. When the ratio is known, the weighted conformal threshold is semiparametrically efficient if and only if the ratio and the coverage indicator are uncorrelated under the test distribution, with an explicit efficient correction otherwise. When $χ^2(Q\|P)=\infty$, the ratio has a regularly varying tail of index $p\in(1,2)$ and the score decouples from it in the far tail, the finite-dimensional limits are $p$-stable at the rate $m^{1-1/p}$ up to a slowly varying factor.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Approximate Factor Models with Score-Driven Dynamics: Estimation and Inference
papers.abstract: We propose a factor model for high-dimensional time series where the dynamics of the latent factors is generated by a multivariate score-driven model, thus allowing to model nonlinearities and heavy tails in both the conditional mean and the conditional variance. Estimation is in two steps: first the factors are extracted via Principal Components and then the parameters of the score-driven model are estimated via Quasi Maximum Likelihood based on the estimated factors. Since factors are not identified, we first establish set-consistency and asymptotic normality for the estimated parameters governing their dynamics, as both the number of time series and the sample size diverge to infinity. Then, we construct valid asymptotic prediction intervals, which do not depend on the chosen identifying constraints for the factors. Numerical results confirm the goodness of our estimator.

papers.title: Testing Cross-Sectional Dependence in Clustered Data
papers.abstract: In clustered data, cross-sectional dependence within clusters can be characterized as weak, semi-strong, or strong. This paper proposes a simple test to identify the specific nature of this dependence in linear regression models. By exploiting the variation in cluster sizes, our approach detects the underlying dependence structure in a computationally simple and robust manner. We develop a test statistic that is shown to be asymptotically chi-square distributed under the null hypothesis of weak dependence. Simulation studies and an empirical illustration using India's Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) data for 2022-23 demonstrate the usefulness of the proposed test.

papers.title: orderStatMoments: Exact Means, Variances, and Covariances of Order Statistics in R
papers.abstract: Calculating the moments, i.e., means, variances, and covariances, of the order statistics of a sample is critical, as they are foundations for order-statistics-based estimation and inference problems. In the early literature, the exact covariance matrices were tabulated only up to the sample size of 50 under normality. Recent software either provides exact calculation only for the means and variances of single order statistics, or obtains the covariances by approximations. We create the R package orderStatMoments to calculate the exact values of these moments for any ranks and any sample size. It covers thirteen built-in distribution families, specified by name and parameters as in R, and allows for continuous distributions defined by the user under relatively weak conditions. It also calculates the moments of any linear combination of order statistics, including sample quantiles, and Lloyd's best linear unbiased estimators with their variances. The work makes two contributions. First, the package provides the exact covariances between order statistics, which no software we found does. Second, we design methods based on the statistical properties of order statistics critical for ultra accurate computing at large sample sizes and various distributions. The accuracy is verified against closed forms at sample sizes up to $n = 10^6$, against the permutation identities on full matrices, and against 556 cells tabulated in seven publications, where it identified some errors far beyond the stated accuracy. A comparison with five R packages and Python's SciPy shows advantages of this package. Computing is efficient, with a time nearly independent of the sample size.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Fractional Load Forecasting With Memory-Aware Break Detection for Reserve Scheduling
papers.abstract: Day-ahead load forecasts set balancing reserves, including the energy a pumped-storage plant holds against forecast errors. Both depend on three effects that are usually modeled separately, namely the thermal inertia of buildings, which makes load lag temperature, structural breaks, which shift demand, and the long memory of forecast errors, which keeps them from cancelling out. We prove that averaging building responses over Cole-Cole distributed time constants yields a fractional temperature kernel with nonnegative weights exactly when its order is at most one. A Bayesian information criterion that ignores long memory selects spurious breaks with probability tending to one, so breaks and memory are estimated jointly, and an online break detector keeps its false-alarm rate below any prescribed level. Long memory also makes the required storage energy grow faster than the square root of the horizon, so a second-order cone program schedules reserves from the joint distribution of hourly errors. On New England and Mid-Atlantic data including the 2020 pandemic, the proposed framework improves on the best of ten benchmarks by 15.7% and 10.3% in mean absolute percentage error. Its reserves breach the storage energy limit on 4.1% and 8.5% of days, against 36.7% and 57.5% with error correlations ignored.

papers.title: RADISH: A Robust Covariate-Adaptive Trial Design with Historical Control Borrowing
papers.abstract: Incorporating historical controls into randomized clinical trials can improve statistical efficiency and alleviate enrollment challenges by reducing the need for concurrent controls, particularly when their recruitment is ethically or logistically challenging. These gains depend on comparability between the historical and concurrent controls. Many dynamic borrowing methods assess compatibility for the overall study populations and apply the same borrowing decision to every participant, even when comparability varies with participant covariates. We propose RADISH, Robust Adaptive Discrepancy-Informed Shrinkage for Historical Borrowing, a covariate-adaptive design that assesses compatibility at the individual participant level and incorporates robust borrowing into sequential randomization and final inference. Under the stated regularity conditions, the RADISH estimator is asymptotically normal and supports asymptotically valid Wald inference. Simulation studies, including semi-synthetic simulation studies based on the two real-world randomized trials, show that RADISH improves efficiency and assigns fewer participants to the control group when the historical and concurrent controls are compatible. As incompatibility increases, RADISH progressively reduces borrowing and approaches a concurrent-only design and analysis.

papers.title: Subarchetypal Analysis: A Semi-Supervised Framework for Archetypal Analysis
papers.abstract: In this work, we introduce subarchetypal analysis, a new semi-supervised framework for Archetype Analysis (AA) and Archetypoid Analysis (ADA) based on subsets of observations from which archetypal profiles are generated. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first subset-constrained framework for archetypal analysis. Classical AA and ADA are recovered as special cases, and the location result for archetypes is extended to the proposed framework. The generating subsets may be defined a priori by the user to incorporate external knowledge, or determined from intrinsic properties of the data or the underlying problem structure. As an illustration of the latter, we consider efficient subarchetypes within Data Envelopment Analysis, where the subsets are determined by the geometry of the efficient frontier. We develop and implement algorithms for subarchetypal analysis in both multivariate and functional settings, available in an R package. The proposed methods are compared with constrained clustering, group-wise archetypal analysis, and classical unconstrained AA and ADA, and their practical usefulness is demonstrated through applications to business, sports analytics, and human development data.

papers.title: Count Constraints and Conditional Benchmarks for Roster-Based Network Reconstruction
papers.abstract: When everyone reports contact counts for known groups, roster-based aggregated relational data (ARD) can determine individual links. In our sparse circular design with 40 nodes and eight groups, the complete counts fix 35.6% of realized edges on average. Zero counts alone exclude 91.1% of nonedges on average, and the full set of counts raises that share to 91.7%. We assess ranking on the unresolved pairs by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Uniform weighting of compatible graphs yields higher mean AUC than the direct scores from either a circular latent-position fit or a nuclear-norm fit. In a follow-up analysis, using the same fitted probabilities to weight compatible graphs reverses the comparison for the circular fit. With the generating circular form and interaction strength supplied, its mean AUC exceeds uniform by 0.016-0.019 across three paired density settings. The gain is 0.007 under a stochastic blockmodel, where the circular form is misspecified. Nuclear-norm plug-in scores remain below uniform in mean AUC. For independent Bernoulli edges with fixed probabilities strictly between zero and one, we characterize when an oracle using the true probabilities gives the same edge marginals as uniform weighting for every feasible count array. This occurs exactly when the conditional graph law is uniform on every such array, or equivalently when log odds are additive in node-by-group effects. We recommend reporting fixed edge states, ranking on unresolved pairs, and generating-probability error separately.

papers.title: Hermitian Positive Definite Neural Networks for Matrix-CFAR Geometric Signal Detection in Nonhomogeneous Clutter
papers.abstract: Matrix information geometry (MIG) detectors exploit the Riemannian geometry of Hermitian positive definite (HPD) matrices to achieve robust object detection in nonhomogeneous clutter. The matrix constant false alarm rate (matrix-CFAR) method is a representative MIG detector that relies on the geometric structures with respect to specific metrics. In most cases, computing representative HPD covariance matrices requires numerical methods, typically involving computationally intensive iterative optimization algorithms. Although explicit formulas are available for certain cases, such as the log-Euclidean (LE) mean, they are generally unavailable for many other matrix means and medians. To address this challenge, we propose integrating the Hermitian positive definite neural network (HPDNet) into the matrix-CFAR framework, replacing conventional numerical optimization procedures with a learned, geometry-preserving mapping that directly estimates representative HPD covariance matrices from data. In the simulations, the framework is evaluated for MIG detectors using both means and medians associated with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric, the LE metric, and the Bures--Wasserstein metric, on both simulated compound-Gaussian clutter and real IPIX sea clutter. In both cases, the HPDNet is trained solely on simulated data to assess its applicability to the study of real data. The results show a significant reduction of computational cost in testing, while maintaining detection performance and robustness.
